portrait-aldous-crane.webp.prompt:
A character portrait in a painterly fantasy-realism style, the classic CRPG portrait look: head and shoulders, three-quarter view, looking at the viewer, dramatic soft key light, a dark, softly painted background. No text, lettering, borders or frames.

Federation art direction: brutalism. Monumental raw-concrete masses, heavy slabs and deep-set windows, stark repeated geometry and hard shadows, grey and white with heraldic banners and crests; architecture built to dwarf the people in it, ordered, imposing and austere.

Art bible for the Calder system. Palette: slate grey, off-white, tan, peach, sky blue and deep navy blue. Lighting: Hard white starlight on a thin sky, with long, clean shadows. Indoors the light is flat and even, panel-white, with a cold blue cast. Signal lamps and heraldic panels give the only warmth, in muted amber. Architecture: Monumental and symmetrical: barracks blocks in strict rows, contractor towers with identical stepped faces, and wide parade-straight avenues that have since been built over crookedly. Stations are armoured, squared-off and flanked by matching gantries. Everything carries numbered bays and painted crests. Materials: Grey armour plate, white-painted steel, poured concrete, tinted glass in narrow slits. Stencilled numbers, brass fittings worn pale, canvas and cord on the contractor side. Dust over everything on the surface and frost on everything in the shade. Mood: Orderly, tired and watchful. Everything is correctly labelled, and the crews who maintain it are short of sleep. A hum of bureaucracy over a thinning garrison. Design language: The Federation's navy design language: disciplined, symmetrical and armoured, in grey and white. Heraldic crests and bay numbers mark every surface. Buildings are monumental in scale even when the staff are few. Uniforms are cut square, worn with a sash or badge of rank, and the fabric is plain and the stitching tidy.

Aldous Crane, Levy clerk, at Calder Station (Calder Station). A heavyset man in his fifties with a soft face and thinning sandy hair. He wears a rumpled brown Compact coat over a grey navy-issue shirt, with ink stains on the cuff. He keeps a tiny brass abacus in his top pocket and fiddles with it when he talks.

Who they are: A Compact clerk, on loan to the levy office. He balances the books that the Ironhulls pay into and the navy takes out of. He is polite to both sides and trusted by neither.

Their people: Calder runs on navy time, with bells and shift signals, and a habit of saying things in the fewest words that will pass inspection. Downsiders, as the surface people call themselves, are contractors' children and grandchildren, proud of their forms and sick of them. Stationers are navy or near enough, and look down on Downsiders. Both look down on through-traffic. Ironhull crews are 'rusters' to the clerks, and the clerks are 'stampers' to the crews, all with a straight face. People are courteous, tired and careful what they put in writing. Dry jokes are about paperwork, because jokes about the war are bad luck. Outsiders who stay polite and keep their papers in order get on well. Outsiders who argue find that the line behind them grows long, and so does the argument.

The background is the dim bar of the port, out of focus, in the system's palette.
